\chapter{Doing, and Undoing}
\label{ch:ta-doing-and-undoing}
\hlchaptermodality{65}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say drink, walk, stop, open and close in Tamil, and name the action that undoes each one.}

Complete TA-C65-doing-recall and produce each of the five doings from the act that undoes it, out of order.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kuḍi]{\ta{குடி} (kuḍi) — drink}

\label{lesson:TA-C65-drink}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{aṟuvaḍai} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{குடி}}
\textbf{\ta{குடி}} (\emph{kuḍi}) — \textquotedblleft{}drink\textquotedblright{}.

You already have \ta{சாப்பிடு} (\emph{sāppiḍu}) for what you chew. \ta{குடி} is what you do to a liquid, and Tamil keeps the two apart the way English does: rice is \ta{சாப்பிடு}, \ta{தண்ணீர்} is \ta{குடி}.

Say what is being drunk, and say it in front of the verb: \textbf{\ta{தண்ணீர்} \ta{குடி}} (\emph{taṇṇīr kuḍi}), \textbf{\ta{தேநீர்} \ta{குடி}} (\emph{tēnīr kuḍi}), \textbf{\ta{பால்} \ta{குடி}} (\emph{pāl kuḍi}). Naming the liquid is not decoration. On its own, without anything in front of it, \ta{குடி} is also the everyday noun for the drinking \emph{habit} — a man described as being given to \ta{குடி} is being described as a drinker. So a speaker who wants the plain, ordinary sense puts the drink in the sentence, and there is nothing left to misread.

Across the family: Kannada uses \ka{ಕುಡಿ} (\emph{kuḍi}) and Malayalam \ml{കുടിക്കുക} (\emph{kuṭikkuka}) — the same word, worn a little differently. Telugu reached for something else entirely and drinks with \te{త్రాగు} (\emph{trāgu}).

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five everyday doings, and the one that completes the pair you had half of.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kuḍi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{taṇṇīr kuḍi} — \textquotedblleft{}drink water\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tēnīr kuḍi}, then \emph{pāl kuḍi}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of \emph{sāppiḍu} and \emph{kuḍi} takes \emph{sādam}, and which takes \emph{taṇṇīr}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vēṇḍukōḷ}, then read \textbf{\ta{நெல்}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{குடி} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}drink\textquotedblright{}.) And what does a speaker put in front of it, every time? (The drink itself.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[naḍa]{\ta{நட} (naḍa) — walk}

\label{lesson:TA-C65-walk}



\begin{quote}
What did \emph{kuḍi} mean, and what does a speaker name in front of it?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நட}}
\textbf{\ta{நட}} (\emph{naḍa}) — \textquotedblleft{}walk\textquotedblright{}.

You have \ta{போ} (\emph{pō}) for going. \ta{போ} says nothing about how — by bus, by train, on foot. \ta{நட} names the feet. Where \ta{போ} leaves the manner open, \ta{நட} fills it in, so the two sit side by side rather than competing: \emph{pō} to leave, \emph{naḍa} to leave on foot.

One neighbour worth hearing apart. You have met \textbf{\ta{நடு}} (\emph{naṭu}, \textquotedblleft{}middle\textquotedblright{}), inside the words for midday and midnight. \textbf{\ta{நட}} and \textbf{\ta{நடு}} differ by the little \textbf{\ta{ு}} hook at the end and by nothing else, and they are two separate words: one is an action, one is a position.

Across the family: this one all four sisters kept. Kannada \ka{ನಡೆ} (\emph{naḍe}), Telugu \te{నడుచు} (\emph{naḍucu}), Malayalam \ml{നടക്കുക} (\emph{naṭakkuka}) — and Tamil \ta{நட}. Where the drinking word split Telugu off, the walking word holds the family together.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two doings. One of them fills in what the other leaves open.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{naḍa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{pō}, then \emph{naḍa}, and say which one names the feet
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{naḍa}, then \emph{naṭu}, and hear the hook arrive
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kuḍi}, then \emph{naḍa}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{அனுமதி}}, then say \emph{pul}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நட} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}walk\textquotedblright{}.) Which of \ta{போ} and \ta{நட} tells you the feet were doing it? (\textbf{\ta{நட}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[kuḍi]{\ta{குடி} — a word with nothing new in it}

\label{lesson:TA-W21-read-kudi}



\begin{quote}
Two lessons ago you learned to say \emph{kuḍi}, and a walking word came between. Now look at it on the page.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: nothing new}
Every lesson in this strand so far has arrived carrying a letter you had not met. This one arrives carrying none. All four pieces of \textbf{\ta{குடி}} are already yours, and the work is putting them together.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{piece} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ta{கு}} & \emph{ku} — \textbf{\ta{க}} with the \textbf{\ta{ு}} sign & \textbf{\ta{க}} from the very first writing lesson; the \textbf{\ta{ு}} hook from \emph{uṇavu} \\
\textbf{\ta{டி}} & \emph{ḍi} — \textbf{\ta{ட}} with the \textbf{\ta{ி}} sign & \textbf{\ta{ட}} from \emph{eppaḍi}; the \textbf{\ta{ி}} sign from \emph{naṉṟi} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ta{கு} · \ta{டி} $\to$ \ta{குடி}}
\end{quote}

Two letters, two signs riding them, and a word you have been saying since the drinking lesson. Nothing here is a new shape; the only new thing is that these four now sit together.

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: the letter you can hear moving}
\textbf{\ta{ட}} is the letter this book writes as \emph{ḍ} here and as \emph{ṭ} elsewhere, because Tamil does not mark the difference on the page — the position in the word decides it. Inside \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}} you say \emph{eppaḍi}, and inside \textbf{\ta{குடி}} you say \emph{kuḍi}: in both, \textbf{\ta{ட}} sits between vowels and softens. The same shape, read by where it stands.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{கு}} — then \textbf{\ta{டி}} — then \textbf{\ta{குடி}}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{\ta{குடி}} and \textbf{\ta{எப்படி}} — find the \textbf{\ta{ட}} in each
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kuḍi}, and name the drink you would put in front of it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Read \textbf{\ta{குடி}}. How many letters carry a vowel sign in it? (Both of them.) What decides whether \textbf{\ta{ட}} comes out \emph{ṭ} or \emph{ḍ}? (Where it stands in the word.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[niṟuttu]{\ta{நிறுத்து} (niṟuttu) — stop}

\label{lesson:TA-C65-stop}



\begin{quote}
Read \textbf{\ta{குடி}} off the page once. Then: what did \emph{naḍa} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{நிறுத்து}}
\textbf{\ta{நிறுத்து}} (\emph{niṟuttu}) — \textquotedblleft{}stop\textquotedblright{}.

This is what undoes \ta{நட}. Feet moving is \emph{naḍa}; \textbf{\ta{நிறுத்து}!} called across a street brings them to a halt, and it is the word for stopping a bus, a song, a clock or an argument as readily as a person.

It is a long word for a short act, and it comes apart. Inside it is the standing-family that gave you \textbf{\ta{நிலை}} (\emph{nilai}, \textquotedblleft{}a state, a standing\textquotedblright{}) — the piece you already met welded into \ta{வானிலை} (\emph{vāṉilai}, \textquotedblleft{}weather\textquotedblright{}), the sky's \emph{standing}. Where \ta{நிலை} names the state, \ta{நிறுத்து} is the making of it: bring the thing to a stand. The weather word and the stopping word are cousins, and knowing that is why \emph{niṟuttu} has somewhere to sit in your memory rather than four syllables to survive on.

Across the family: Kannada \ka{ನಿಲ್ಲಿಸು} (\emph{nillisu}) and Malayalam \ml{നിർത്തുക} (\emph{nirttuka}) are built the same way, from the same standing-verb.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three doings, and the first pair that undoes itself: \emph{naḍa} against \emph{niṟuttu}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{niṟuttu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{naḍa}, then \emph{niṟuttu} — moving, then halted
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{niṟuttu} the way you would call it across a street
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{vāṉilai}, and name the piece of it this verb is related to
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{tayakkam}, then read \textbf{\ta{பயிர்}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{நிறுத்து} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}stop\textquotedblright{}.) Which everyday word already carried its family? (\textbf{\ta{வானிலை}} — the sky's \emph{standing}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tiṟa]{\ta{திற} (tiṟa) — open}

\label{lesson:TA-C65-open}



\begin{quote}
What did \emph{niṟuttu} mean, and which walking word does it undo?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{திற}}
\textbf{\ta{திற}} (\emph{tiṟa}) — \textquotedblleft{}open\textquotedblright{}.

You have \ta{கதவு} (\emph{kadavu}), the door. \ta{திற} is what you do to it. The \textbf{\ta{ற}} in the middle is the hard, tapped \emph{ṟ} you first met in \ta{நன்றி} (\emph{naṉṟi}) — the same letter, in a word where nothing hides it.

Tamil joins a verb to the thing it acts on with an ending this chapter does not open yet, so hold \emph{kadavu} and \emph{tiṟa} as two words you can say in sequence rather than a sentence you can build. The pair is worth having early even without the joint: a door and the act of opening it are two of the first things anyone needs at somebody else's house.

Across the family, one old word in four shapes: Kannada has \ka{ತೆರೆ} (\emph{tere}), Telugu has \te{తెరుచు} (\emph{terucu}), and Malayalam has \ml{തുറക്കുക} (\emph{tuṟakkuka}). Tamil's keeps the tapped \textbf{\ta{ற}} the others softened away.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four doings, and a verb that belongs to a noun you already carry.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tiṟa}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{kadavu}, then \emph{tiṟa} — the thing, then the act
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{naṉṟi}, then \emph{tiṟa}, and hear the same \textbf{\ta{ற}} twice
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{niṟuttu}, then \emph{tiṟa}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\ta{நம்பிக்கை}}, then say \emph{kaḷam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \ta{திற} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}open\textquotedblright{}.) Which door word does it go with? (\textbf{\ta{கதவு}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūḍu]{\ta{மூடு} (mūḍu) — close}

\label{lesson:TA-C65-close}



\begin{quote}
What did \emph{tiṟa} mean, and which noun does it belong beside?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ta{மூடு}}
\textbf{\ta{மூடு}} (\emph{mūḍu}) — \textquotedblleft{}close\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}shut\textquotedblright{}.

The verb that undoes \ta{திற}. A \ta{கதவு} you have opened is a \ta{கதவு} you can \ta{மூடு}, and the two travel together the way \emph{naḍa} and \emph{niṟuttu} do.

The long \textbf{\ta{ூ}} at its front is the same sign you read in \textbf{\ta{மூன்று}} (\emph{mūṉṟu}, \textquotedblleft{}three\textquotedblright{}). Two words, one sign, no relation between their meanings — worth noticing so the shape stops being a surprise.

Across the family, this one did not travel. Kannada shuts a door with \ka{ಮುಚ್ಚು} (\emph{muccu}), Telugu with \te{మూయు} (\emph{mūyu}), and Malayalam with \ml{അടയ്ക്കുക} (\emph{aṭaykkuka}). Four sisters, three different words — after two verbs the family held in common, a reminder that the sharing is real but never guaranteed.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five everyday doings, in pairs: \emph{sāppiḍu} with \emph{kuḍi}, \emph{naḍa} with \emph{niṟuttu}, \emph{tiṟa} with \emph{mūḍu}. Each one arrived beside the act that undoes it, which is the cheapest way there is to hold two words instead of one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mūḍu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tiṟa}, then \emph{mūḍu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five in order — \emph{kuḍi}, \emph{naḍa}, \emph{niṟuttu}, \emph{tiṟa}, \emph{mūḍu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} for each of \emph{naḍa} and \emph{tiṟa}, the word that undoes it
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{taṇṇīr kuḍi}, then \emph{kadavu}, then \emph{mūḍu}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\ta{குடி}} — the one word of the five you have spelled out
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{paṇivu}, then read \textbf{\ta{அறுவடை}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the five doings in order. Which two of them make a pair with a door? (\textbf{\ta{திற}} and \textbf{\ta{மூடு}}.) Which drink word did you put in front of \textbf{\ta{குடி}}? (\emph{taṇṇīr}, or \emph{tēnīr}, or \emph{pāl}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
